- Overestimate prices when sentiment is bullish (sentiment > 0.5) and especially after recent spikes; reduce forecast peak heights.
- Underestimate prices when sentiment is bearish (sentiment < 0.5) or when sentiment is neutral (0.33–0.67) and recent price action shows mean reversion.
- Lagged forecasts tend to overreact to sentiment shifts; adjust for 1–2 day delay in sentiment-driven price movements.
- After a sharp price spike, model often overshoots; cap forecast peaks at 10–15% below the true peak or use moving average smoothing.
- When sentiment is consistently low (e.g., 0.00 or 0.33), model tends to underestimate; add 2–5% buffer to forecast if sentiment is persistently negative.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, model often fails to capture mean reversion; apply a 3–5 day moving average to smooth out overfitting to recent volatility.
- If sentiment is high and price is rising, model often overweights sentiment; reduce forecast sensitivity to sentiment > 0.75.
- When sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67), model tends to overfit recent price trends; use sentiment-weighted average of 3–5 prior days to anchor forecast.
